para_before: Pembrolizumab

Pembrolizumab added JPY 4,426 thousand per patient in costs (95% UI [−330, 8,901]) and 2.156 QALYs (95% UI [0.245, 4.228]), for an ICER of JPY 2,053 thousand per QALY (Table 3). Its drug cost was JPY 6,531 thousand, offset partly by JPY −1,911 thousand in second-line and later treatment of distant recurrence. The probability that it was cost-effective was 83.1% at JPY 5 million and 90.8% at JPY 7.5 million per QALY. The ICER was JPY 3,044 thousand with Japanese post-operative treatment, JPY 2,565 thousand with metastatic treatment costs halved, JPY 2,785 thousand with eribulin-based treatment and JPY 1,920 thousand with higher mortality after early recurrence with pembrolizumab (Table 3).

To gain as many QALYs as pembrolizumab, exercise added to chemotherapy alone required a recurrence HR of 0.425 or an increase in pCR of 35.9 percentage points, both outside the ranges studied (Table 3).

Trial inputs came from KEYNOTE-522 reports with data cutoffs from March 2021 to October 2025 [4,5,43,44], extracted from 21 to 26 October 2026. The analysis plan was written before any economic computation, and each later addition before the computation it added; the plan was not registered. The study follows the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards 2022 (CHEERS 2022) [45]. Supplementary Methods S1, Tables S1–S10 (including the CHEERS checklist in Table S1) and Figs. S1–S2 are in Online Resource 1.

para_before: Exercise during adjuvant chemotherapy improves fitness [10–12], and supervised exercise has been delivered during neoadjuvant chemotherapy [16,17], so clinicians can offer it while its effect on recurrence is tested. Trials should record recurrence and follow patients long enough to see whether the effect lasts after the program ends; a higher pCR alone cannot settle the question, because how a change in pCR with exercise translates into fewer recurrences is unknown. Funders can weigh the cost of such trials against the one-year net benefit if an effect is confirmed (Table S8). For payers, the price of a supervised program is far below what a confirmed effect would justify. In Japan, the fee schedule pays for rehabilitation of patients with cancer only during hospital admission, so structured exercise during outpatient neoadjuvant chemotherapy currently has no route to reimbursement [48]. Support that keeps patients exercising after surgery, such as remote programs, would add value if it extends the effect (Table S7). For pembrolizumab, this analysis gives Japan a reference value before any formal evaluation of its perioperative indication.

para_before: This study estimated, from the perspective of the Japanese public healthcare payer, the maximum cost per patient at which adding a structured exercise program to neoadjuvant chemotherapy with pembrolizumab for stage II or III TNBC would be cost-effective, and how this cost depends on the size and duration of the effect of exercise on recurrence. Secondary aims were to estimate the same cost when exercise is added to chemotherapy alone, to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of pembrolizumab in Japan, and to estimate the effect of exercise that would match the gain in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) from pembrolizumab. Expressing the value of an unproven program as the cost a health system can afford for each possible effect gives future trials a benchmark for their results.
para_after: This study aimed to place a structured exercise program during neoadjuvant chemotherapy for stage II or III TNBC on the same cost-effectiveness scale as pembrolizumab, from the perspective of the Japanese public healthcare payer. It compared the four strategies formed by chemotherapy with or without pembrolizumab and with or without exercise; it asked how large an effect on recurrence exercise would need to match pembrolizumab, in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and in net benefit; and, as its main aim, it estimated the maximum cost per patient at which exercise added to chemotherapy with pembrolizumab would be cost-effective, and how this cost depends on the size and duration of the effect of exercise on recurrence. Expressing the value of an unproven program as the cost a health system can afford for each possible effect gives future trials a benchmark for their results.

para_before: Secondary outcomes were the recurrence HRs at which the maximum affordable cost, or the medical costs avoided, equaled the cost of a program; the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of pembrolizumab against chemotherapy alone; the exercise effect, as a recurrence HR or an increase in pCR, that would gain as many QALYs as pembrolizumab; and the one-year net benefit, the maximum affordable cost minus the program cost summed over eligible patients treated in Japan in one year.
para_after: Secondary outcomes were the total costs and QALYs of the four arms and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) between them at recurrence HRs of 0.95, 0.85 and 0.72; the ICER of pembrolizumab against chemotherapy alone; the exercise effect, as a recurrence HR or an increase in pCR, at which exercise added to chemotherapy alone would gain as many QALYs as pembrolizumab, or the same net monetary benefit, the QALYs gained valued at the threshold minus the incremental cost; the recurrence HRs at which the maximum affordable cost, or the medical costs avoided, equaled the cost of a program; and the one-year net benefit, the maximum affordable cost minus the program cost summed over eligible patients treated in Japan in one year.

Four strategies compared

Table 2 shows the four strategies at recurrence HRs with exercise of 0.95, 0.85 and 0.72, with the fee-schedule-based program. At each HR, chemotherapy plus exercise cost less and gave more QALYs than chemotherapy alone, and chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab plus exercise cost less and gave more QALYs than chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab, so both strategies without exercise were dominated. Adding pembrolizumab to chemotherapy plus exercise cost JPY 2,112 thousand per QALY at an HR of 0.95, JPY 2,245 thousand at 0.85 and JPY 2,449 thousand at 0.72. Relative to chemotherapy alone, the net monetary benefit of exercise at JPY 5 million per QALY was JPY 931 thousand at an HR of 0.95, JPY 3,250 thousand at 0.85 and JPY 6,413 thousand at 0.72, against JPY 6,355 thousand for pembrolizumab. Chemotherapy with both had the highest net monetary benefit at every HR.
Exercise compared with pembrolizumab

Table 2 also shows pembrolizumab against chemotherapy alone: it cost JPY 4,426 thousand more per patient (95% UI [−330, 8,901]) and added 2.156 QALYs (95% UI [0.245, 4.228]), an ICER of JPY 2,053 thousand per QALY, and it was cost-effective in 83.1% of probabilistic samples at JPY 5 million and 90.8% at JPY 7.5 million per QALY. Its drug cost of JPY 6,531 thousand was offset partly by JPY −1,911 thousand in second-line and later treatment of distant recurrence (Table S4). To gain as many QALYs as pembrolizumab, exercise added to chemotherapy alone required a recurrence HR of 0.425 or an increase in pCR of 35.9 percentage points (Table 2). To give the same net monetary benefit with the fee-schedule-based program, it required an HR of 0.722 or an increase in pCR of 19.0 percentage points at JPY 5 million per QALY, and an HR of 0.638 or an increase of 24.1 percentage points at JPY 7.5 million. Except the HR of 0.722, these values lay outside the ranges studied.

para_before: Whether exercise during neoadjuvant chemotherapy for stage II or III TNBC reduces recurrence is unknown. If it does, even a small effect would make a structured program cost-effective in Japan: with chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab, the fee-schedule-based program became cost-effective once it lowered the recurrence hazard by 1.1%. How much a program could cost depended mostly on how large its effect was and how long it lasted, and pembrolizumab itself was cost-effective at both Japanese thresholds.
para_after: At each of the three effect sizes examined, both strategies without exercise were dominated (Table 2), so the choice in Japan is not between exercise and pembrolizumab. Pembrolizumab remained cost-effective on top of exercise, and chemotherapy with both gave the most health for the money at every effect size.

Exercise cannot replace pembrolizumab in health gained: it would need to lower the recurrence hazard by more than half, far beyond the effects reported in exercise trials [9,14]. In value for money the gap is narrower, because the program costs a small fraction of the pembrolizumab regimen. At the Japanese threshold, exercise added to chemotherapy alone would give the same net benefit as pembrolizumab with an effect the size of that in CHALLENGE, a 28% reduction in the recurrence hazard, and at the higher threshold reserved for designated products pembrolizumab keeps its lead unless exercise cuts the hazard by more than a third. The effect of pembrolizumab is established and that of exercise is not, so a payer choosing one would still choose pembrolizumab; the comparison shows how much health a cheap program could buy if its effect were confirmed.

For patients who receive pembrolizumab, now most patients in Japan [7], the question is what a program added to their treatment may cost. Whether exercise during neoadjuvant chemotherapy for stage II or III TNBC reduces recurrence is unknown; if it does, even a small effect would make a structured program cost-effective: the fee-schedule-based program became cost-effective once it lowered the recurrence hazard by 1.1%. How much a program could cost depended mostly on how large its effect was and how long it lasted.

Pembrolizumab was cost-effective in Japan, as in other countries [28–31], and depended most on its price and on post-operative capecitabine or olaparib as used in Japanese practice.
